High intra-abdominal pressure can trigger uterine cramps. Swap heavy squats or deadlifts for light dumbbells, upper body form work, and pelvic mobility.

Peak estrogen coupled with a minor testosterone surge. Prime window for heavy compound lifts (Squat, Deadlift, Hip Thrust) in the 3–5 rep strength range.
Neuromuscular power peaks, but peak estrogen relaxes ligament collagen. Control eccentric lowering and avoid knee valgus (knee caving) on heavy lifts.
Progesterone elevates resting core temperature by +0.3–0.5°C. Focus on controlled tempo, supersets, and isolation exercises rather than max singles.
Fluid retention can create joint stiffness and increase perceived exertion (RPE). Transition to cable and machine exercises (Leg Press, Cable Rows) for joint safety.
Hormone withdrawal accelerates muscle catabolism and strains CNS recovery. Drop working weights by 40–50%, keep sessions under 40 mins, and consume protein with leucine immediately post-workout.
Avoid heavy intra-abdominal bracing (valsalva) that exacerbates cramps.
⚠️ ACL Caution: Estrogen surge relaxes ligaments. Spend 5–7 min on knee/glute stabilization warmup.
Core temperature is higher (+0.5°C). You sweat earlier; consume cold electrolyte water.

Catabolic Alert: Elevated protein breakdown. Consume 25–30g protein with leucine within 30 min post-workout.

• Est. 1RM (One-Rep Max): The heaviest weight you could theoretically lift for 1 repetition, calculated from your best multi-rep set using the Epley formula.\n• Relative Strength (x BW): Your 1RM divided by your body weight. If this ratio climbs, you are gaining true neuromuscular strength regardless of scale fluctuations.
💧 Cycle Edema Note: Temporary +1–2 kg water retention in the Luteal or Menstrual phase can slightly lower your x BW ratio on paper even when your actual muscle strength hasn't dropped.

All strength, tonnage, and fluid-retention calculations run 100% offline on your device using validated sports science equations and clinical physiology literature.

Estimated One-Repetition Maximum is computed via the Epley linear equation: 1RM = Weight × (1 + Reps / 30). Validated by LeSuer et al. (1997, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 11(4), 211–213; DOI: 10.1519/00124278-199711000-00001), demonstrating r ≥ 0.95 correlation with actual tested 1RM across the Squat (r = 0.97), Bench Press (r = 0.99), and Deadlift (r = 0.95).
Relative Strength & Normative Tiers — Suchomel et al. (2016) & NSCA

Dividing 1RM by current body weight (1RM / BW) isolates true neuromuscular efficiency from scale weight fluctuations (Suchomel, Nimphius, & Stone, 2016, Sports Medicine, 46(10), 1419–1449; PMID: 26838985). Sex-stratified tiers (Starter, Intermediate, Advanced, Elite) are calibrated from NSCA (Haff & Triplett, 2016, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning) and Rippetoe, Kilgore, & Pendlay (2006, Practical Programming for Strength Training).
DOMS Edema & Glycogen Hydration — Peake et al. (2017) & Kreitzman et al. (1992)

High-volume eccentric loading triggers sarcomere micro-trauma and acute inflammatory extracellular fluid retention for 24–72h (Peake et al., 2017, J Appl Physiol, 122(3), 559–570, PMID: 28035017; Clarkson & Hubal, 2002, Am J Phys Med Rehabil, 81(11), S52–S69, PMID: 12409811). Simultaneously, muscle glycogen resynthesis binds 3–4g of intracellular water per 1g of glycogen (Kreitzman et al., 1992, Am J Clin Nutr, PMID: 1615908; Fernández-Elías et al., 2015, Eur J Appl Physiol, PMID: 25911631).
Volume Load & RIR-RPE Autoregulation — Schoenfeld et al. (2017) & Helms et al. (2016)

Session tonnage (Sets × Reps × Weight) tracks the graded dose-response between weekly training volume and skeletal muscle hypertrophy (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, & Krieger, 2017, J Sports Sci, 35(11), 1073–1082; PMID: 27433992). Exertion analysis utilizes the Repetitions in Reserve (RIR)-based RPE scale to quantify CNS fatigue and autoregulate load (Helms et al., 2016, Strength Cond J, 38(4), 42–49; PMID: 27531969).

Exercise Performance & Strength Meta-Analysis (McNulty et al., 2020)

Systematic review of 78 studies (Sports Medicine, 50(10), 1813–1827; PMID: 32661870) mapping how estradiol and progesterone fluctuations across the cycle influence neuromuscular force, recovery kinetics, and individualized training readiness.

Endocrine physiology research (Exerc Sport Sci Rev, 36(3), 152–159; PMID: 18580296) detailing how luteal progesterone and estradiol activate the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and shift osmotic thresholds, causing temporary +1–2.5 kg extracellular water retention on the scale.
Luteal Thermoregulation & Basal Metabolic Rate (Baker et al., 2020; Solomon et al., 1982)

Clinical evidence on progesterone's hypothalamic thermogenic shift (+0.3–0.5°C core temperature; Temperature, 7(3), 226–262, PMID: 33123618) and luteal resting metabolic rate elevation (+100–250 kcal/day; Am J Clin Nutr, 36(4), 611–616, PMID: 7124662; PLOS ONE, PMID: 32658929), explaining higher luteal RPE and caloric needs.
Ovulatory ACL Laxity & ACOG Guidelines (Herzberg et al., 2017; ACOG, 2023)

Meta-analysis of 68,758 participants (Orthop J Sports Med, 5(7); PMID: 28795075) confirming estrogen-induced anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) laxity peaks during ovulation, paired with ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 7 (Obstet Gynecol, 142(6), 1516–1533; PMID: 37973069) on prostaglandin cramping, iron replacement, and PMS management.
